result.summary: Pausanias describes Stymphelus in Arcadia, its ancient founder and the tradition of Hera's three temples, and its spring and river that goes underground. He discusses the man-eating Stymphelian birds and Hercules, the Arabian birds of the same name, the temple of Stymphelian Artemis, and a flood that ended when a hunter and deer vanished into a chasm.

scenes.title: Stymphelus and Hera's temples
scenes.summary: Pausanias returns to Stymphelus, notes its Arcadian origin, and tells how Temenus raised Hera and built three temples to her.

scenes.title: The spring, river and birds
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the spring, the river that sinks and reappears as the Erasinus, and the birds that Hercules killed or scared away, comparing them with Arabian birds.
scenes.stakes: People on the river banks are in danger from the man-eating birds.

scenes.title: Temple of Stymphelian Artemis
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the old temple, its gilded wooden statue, the bird images on the roof and the bird-legged maidens behind.

scenes.title: The flood and the hunter
scenes.summary: During a careless festival a fallen tree blocks the river's chasm and floods the plain, until a hunter and deer fall in and the water drains. The festival is afterwards kept with more zeal.
scenes.stakes: The plain is flooded, and the hunter is swallowed by the chasm.

alias_notes.explanation: Title Temenus gave Hera after she left Zeus.

analysis.text: Pausanias weighs local myth against rational explanation, such as whether the birds came from Arabia, while recording cult details and religious duty.
The mention of Hadrian's aqueduct to Corinth shows Roman imperial building in Greece, and the Argolic League note shows Arcadia's changed political ties.

legacy.text: The Stymphalian birds became one of the labours of Hercules, often depicted in Greek and later art.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias admits he cannot tell whether the roof birds are wood or plaster, a sign of his careful eyewitness style.

language_notes.text: The Argolic League means the federation centred on Argos; the Stymphelians had chosen to join it rather than the Arcadian communities.
The three titles are the cult epithets of Hera: Child (Pais), Full-grown (Teleia), and Widow (Chera). The text gives the names in English translation.
Pisander of Camirus was an early Greek epic poet who wrote a Heracles poem. Pausanias cites him for a rival version of the labour.
Bird-lime is a sticky substance smeared on twigs to trap small birds.
A stade (stadion) was a Greek unit of length, roughly 180–200 metres, so the flooded area is described by its circuit.
The italicised clause explains the draining: the hunter and deer, by falling in, cleared the blocked passage so the water could escape.

context_notes.text: Adrian is the Roman emperor Hadrian (ruled AD 117–138), who built many public works, including aqueducts, in Greek cities.
Pausanias reports the belief that the river flows underground and re-emerges in Argolis as the Erasinus.
Killing the Stymphalian birds was one of the labours of Hercules.
Artemis was the goddess of hunting and wild places, so her cult at a marshy, bird-haunted spring is fitting.

literary_notes.text: The wings of little birds stuck in bird-lime vividly compare easy penetration of thick matting to helpless entanglement.
Pausanias reasons cautiously as a scholar-traveller, admitting ignorance and offering a speculative theory about the birds' origin.
The flood punishes careless worship, and the closing note of renewed zeal gives the story a moral about piety.
